৯) Drug induced lupus is associated with following antibodies
Medicine-09.exp:
Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is classically associated with anti-histone antibodies, which are present in >95% of cases. Common causative drugs include:

  • Hydralazine

  • Procainamide

  • Isoniazid

  • Methyldopa

  • Minocycline

  • Quinidine

Unlike idiopathic SLE, renal and CNS involvement are uncommon, and symptoms usually resolve after discontinuation of the offending drug.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Anti-Ro (SSA) — Associated with Sjögren syndrome, neonatal lupus, and congenital heart block.

  • B. Anti-La (SSB) — Associated with Sjögren syndrome and neonatal lupus.

  • C. Anti-histone antibody — Correct. Characteristic antibody in drug-induced lupus.

  • D. Anti-RNP antibody — Associated with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD).

High-yield Recall

Autoantibody Disease/Association
Anti-histone Drug-induced lupus
Anti-dsDNA SLE, lupus nephritis
Anti-Sm Specific for SLE
Anti-Ro (SSA) Neonatal lupus, congenital heart block, Sjögren syndrome
Anti-RNP Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD)

Exam pearl: Drug-induced lupus → Anti-histone antibodies; SLE → Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Sm antibodies.

Medicine-09.question: ১০) ‘Watermelon’ stomach is found in
Medicine-09.exp:
"Watermelon stomach" refers to Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE), characterized by longitudinal red streaks in the gastric antrum resembling the stripes of a watermelon on endoscopy.

It is classically associated with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) and can cause chronic gastrointestinal bleeding leading to iron deficiency anemia.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Systemic sclerosis — Correct. Classical association with GAVE (watermelon stomach).

  • B. Dermatomyositis — Associated with inflammatory myopathy and malignancy, not watermelon stomach.

  • C. Kawasaki disease — A medium-vessel vasculitis affecting children; not associated with GAVE.

  • D. Polyarteritis nodosa — Medium-vessel vasculitis causing renal, gastrointestinal, and neurological involvement, not watermelon stomach.

High-yield Recall

Condition Characteristic Association
Systemic sclerosis Watermelon stomach (GAVE)
Systemic sclerosis Esophageal dysmotility, GERD
Systemic sclerosis Sclerodactyly, Raynaud phenomenon
Systemic sclerosis Pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension

Exam pearl: Watermelon stomach = Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE) = Systemic sclerosis.

Medicine-09.question: ১১) Features of reactive arthritis excludes
Medicine-09.exp:
Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome) is a seronegative spondyloarthritis that typically develops 1–4 weeks after a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection.

The classical triad is:

  • Arthritis

  • Urethritis

  • Conjunctivitis

Hence, proctitis is not a classical feature of reactive arthritis.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Urethritis — Classical feature of reactive arthritis.

  • B. Arthritis — Hallmark manifestation, usually asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs.

  • C. Conjunctivitis — Classical extra-articular feature.

  • D. Proctitis — Correct. Not part of the classical triad.

High-yield Recall

Reactive Arthritis Features
Arthritis Asymmetric, lower limb oligoarthritis
Urethritis Common preceding GU infection
Conjunctivitis/Uveitis Typical ocular manifestation
HLA-B27 Frequently positive
Common triggers Chlamydia, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter

Exam pearl: "Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree" = Conjunctivitis + Urethritis + Arthritis = Reactive arthritis.

Medicine-09.question: ১২) Triad of anemia, jaundice & splenomegaly are found in
১৩) Visual function monitoring is required in which type of DMARDs
Medicine-09.exp:
Hydroxychloroquine can cause retinal toxicity (bull's-eye maculopathy), which may lead to irreversible visual loss. Therefore, patients taking hydroxychloroquine require:

  • Baseline ophthalmologic examination

  • Regular visual function monitoring (typically annual screening after 5 years of therapy, or earlier in high-risk patients)

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Sulfasalazine — Requires CBC and liver function monitoring, not routine visual monitoring.

  • B. Hydroxychloroquine — Correct. Requires regular ophthalmologic (visual) monitoring.

  • C. Mycophenolate mofetil — Requires CBC and liver/renal function monitoring.

  • D. Azathioprine — Requires CBC, liver function tests, and TPMT/NUDT15 assessment before therapy.

High-yield Recall

DMARD Important Monitoring
Hydroxychloroquine Eye examination (retinal toxicity)
Methotrexate CBC, LFT, RFT
Sulfasalazine CBC, LFT
Azathioprine CBC, LFT, TPMT/NUDT15
Mycophenolate mofetil CBC, LFT, RFT

Exam pearl: Hydroxychloroquine → Retinal toxicity (bull's-eye maculopathy) → Regular ophthalmologic screening is mandatory.

Medicine-09.question: ১৪) The most important risk factors for NSAID-induced ulcers
Medicine-09.option3: Past history of adverse event with NSAID
Medicine-09.exp:
The strongest and most important risk factor for NSAID-induced peptic ulcers and ulcer complications (bleeding/perforation) is a past history of peptic ulcer, especially a previous complicated ulcer (bleeding or perforation).

Other important risk factors include:

  • Age >65 years

  • High-dose or multiple NSAID use

  • Concomitant glucocorticoids

  • Anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs

  • Helicobacter pylori infection

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. High-risk NSAID use — Increases the risk but is not the strongest predictor.

  • B. Concomitant glucocorticoid use — Increases ulcer risk when combined with NSAIDs but is less important than a previous ulcer history.

  • C. Past history of adverse event with NSAID — Suggests intolerance but is not the principal established risk factor for ulcer development.

  • D. Past history of peptic ulcer — Correct. The most important risk factor, particularly if there was previous ulcer bleeding or perforation.

High-yield Recall

Risk Factor Risk of NSAID-Induced Ulcer
Previous peptic ulcer (especially complicated) Highest risk
Age >65 years Increased risk
High-dose/multiple NSAIDs Increased risk
Concomitant glucocorticoids Increased risk
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets Increased risk
H. pylori infection Increased risk

Exam pearl: The greatest predictor of NSAID-related ulcer complications is a previous history of peptic ulcer, especially previous ulcer bleeding.

Medicine-09.question: ১৫) Antibiotic of choice in septic arthritis
Medicine-09.exp:
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis in adults. In areas with a low prevalence of MRSA, the first-line empirical antibiotic is flucloxacillin, which provides excellent coverage against methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) and streptococci.

Treatment also requires urgent joint aspiration/drainage in addition to antibiotics.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Vancomycin — Reserved for suspected or confirmed MRSA infection or severe β-lactam allergy.

  • B. Clindamycin — Alternative in penicillin allergy; not the routine first-line drug.

  • C. Flucloxacillin — Correct. First-line empirical treatment for MSSA septic arthritis.

  • D. Ciprofloxacin — Used mainly for selected Gram-negative infections; not the empirical drug of choice.

High-yield Recall

Clinical Scenario Preferred Antibiotic
Septic arthritis (MSSA suspected) Flucloxacillin
Suspected MRSA Vancomycin
Penicillin allergy Clindamycin (or according to local guidelines)
Gonococcal arthritis Ceftriaxone

Exam pearl: Adult septic arthritis is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus; start empirical flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA is suspected) and perform prompt joint drainage.

Medicine-09.question: ১৬) Type of Hodgkin’s lymphoma with best prognosis
১৭) Highly specific for RA
Medicine-09.exp:
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP) antibodies are highly specific (≈95–98%) for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and may become positive before the onset of clinical disease. They are also associated with more severe and erosive disease.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. ANA — Sensitive for connective tissue diseases but not specific for RA.

  • B. Rheumatoid factor (RF) — Sensitive but less specific; can be positive in other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections, and even healthy elderly individuals.

  • C. Anti-CCP antibodies — Correct. Most specific serological marker for RA.

  • D. Anti-dsDNA — Highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

High-yield Recall

Antibody Disease Association
Anti-CCP Most specific for rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid factor (RF) Sensitive but less specific for RA
ANA Screening test for connective tissue diseases
Anti-dsDNA Specific for SLE, especially lupus nephritis
Anti-Sm Highly specific for SLE

Exam pearl:

  • Most specific antibody for RA: Anti-CCP

  • Most sensitive antibody for RA: Rheumatoid factor (RF) (though less specific)

Medicine-09.question: ১৮) Anisocytosis is related to which feature of RBC?
Medicine-09.exp:
Anisocytosis refers to variation in the size of red blood cells (RBCs). It is commonly seen in:

  • Iron deficiency anemia

  • Megaloblastic anemia

  • Mixed nutritional deficiencies

  • Following blood transfusion

It is reflected by an increased Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW) on a complete blood count.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Size — Correct. Anisocytosis means variation in RBC size.

  • B. Shape — Variation in shape is called poikilocytosis.

  • C. Number — RBC number is assessed by the RBC count, not anisocytosis.

  • D. Colour — Variation in colour (hemoglobin content) is described as hypochromia or polychromasia, not anisocytosis.

High-yield Recall

Term Meaning
Anisocytosis Variation in RBC size
Poikilocytosis Variation in RBC shape
Hypochromia Decreased RBC colour (↓ hemoglobin)
Polychromasia Increased bluish immature RBCs (reticulocytes)

Exam pearl:

  • Anisocytosis = Size variation

  • Poikilocytosis = Shape variation

Medicine-09.question: ১৯) Highly specific for SLE
Medicine-09.exp:
Anti-double-stranded DNA (Anti-dsDNA) antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (specificity >95%). Their levels often correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. ANA — Highly sensitive for SLE (>95%) but not specific.

  • B. RA (Rheumatoid factor) — Associated mainly with rheumatoid arthritis; not specific for SLE.

  • C. Anti-CCP antibodies — Highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

  • D. Anti-dsDNA antibodies — Correct. Highly specific for SLE and associated with lupus nephritis.

High-yield Recall

Autoantibody Disease Association
Anti-dsDNA Highly specific for SLE; correlates with lupus nephritis
Anti-Sm Most specific for SLE (less sensitive)
ANA Most sensitive screening test for SLE
Anti-CCP Most specific for rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid factor (RF) Sensitive but less specific for rheumatoid arthritis

Exam pearl:

  • Most sensitive test for SLE: ANA

  • Highly specific test for SLE: Anti-dsDNA (and Anti-Sm is also highly specific, with the highest specificity but lower sensitivity).

Medicine-09.question: ২০) Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is mostly due to
Medicine-09.exp:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a clonal (monoclonal) malignancy of mature B lymphocytes. It is the most common leukemia in adults in Western countries and is characterized by:

  • Monoclonal proliferation of mature B cells

  • Persistent lymphocytosis

  • Bone marrow, lymph node, and spleen infiltration

  • Immunophenotype: CD5+, CD19+, CD20 (dim), CD23+

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Polyclonal proliferation of B-cell lymphocytes — Reactive process, not leukemia.

  • B. Monoclonal proliferation of B-cell lymphocytes — Correct. Characteristic of CLL.

  • C. Monoclonal proliferation of T-cell lymphocytes — Seen in T-cell leukemias/lymphomas, not typical CLL.

  • D. Polyclonal proliferation of T-cell lymphocytes — Reactive condition, not CLL.

High-yield Recall

Feature Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
Cell of origin Monoclonal mature B lymphocyte
Common age Elderly (>60 years)
Peripheral blood Absolute lymphocytosis, smudge cells
Immunophenotype CD5+, CD19+, CD20(dim), CD23+
Common complication Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, infections

Exam pearl: CLL = Monoclonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes + Smudge cells + CD5 and CD23 positivity.

Medicine-09.question: ২১) Denatured hemoglobin in G6PD deficiency is visible as
Medicine-09.exp:
In G6PD deficiency, oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and precipitate, forming Heinz bodies. These are visible with supravital stains (e.g., crystal violet or brilliant cresyl blue).

As splenic macrophages remove Heinz bodies from RBCs, bite cells (degmacytes) are formed and become visible on the peripheral blood smear.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Bite cells — Formed after splenic removal of Heinz bodies; they do not represent the denatured hemoglobin itself.

  • B. Blister cells — May be seen in G6PD deficiency but are not the denatured hemoglobin.

  • C. Heinz bodies — Correct. These are precipitated (denatured) hemoglobin.

  • D. Basophilic stippling — Seen in lead poisoning, thalassemia, and sideroblastic anemia.

High-yield Recall

Finding Association
Heinz bodies Denatured hemoglobin in G6PD deficiency
Bite cells (Degmacytes) Splenic removal of Heinz bodies
Blister cells Early oxidative RBC injury
Basophilic stippling Lead poisoning, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia

Exam pearl:
G6PD deficiency → Oxidative stress → Heinz bodies (supravital stain) → Bite cells (peripheral blood smear).

Medicine-09.question: ২২) Most common variety of leukaemia
Medicine-09.exp:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the most common leukemia in adults, particularly in the elderly (age >60 years). It is characterized by:

  • Monoclonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes

  • Persistent lymphocytosis

  • Smudge cells on peripheral blood smear

  • Immunophenotype: CD5+, CD19+, CD23+

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. AML — Most common acute leukemia in adults, but not the most common leukemia overall.

  • B. CML — Less common than CLL.

  • C. ALL — Most common leukemia in children, not adults.

  • D. CLL — Correct. Most common leukemia in adults.

High-yield Recall

Leukemia High-yield Fact
CLL Most common leukemia in adults
ALL Most common leukemia in children
AML Most common acute leukemia in adults
CML Associated with BCR-ABL (Philadelphia chromosome)

Exam pearl:

  • Adults: CLL = most common leukemia.

  • Children: ALL = most common leukemia.

  • Acute leukemia in adults: AML = most common.

Medicine-09.question: ২৩) Dimorphic blood picture mostly suggests
Medicine-09.exp:
A dimorphic blood picture means the presence of two distinct populations of red blood cells, typically:

  • Microcytic hypochromic RBCs

  • Normocytic or macrocytic RBCs

It is classically seen in sideroblastic anaemia, although it may also occur:

  • After blood transfusion

  • During treatment of iron deficiency

  • In combined iron and vitamin B12/folate deficiency

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Anaemia of chronic disease — Usually normocytic or mildly microcytic; dimorphic picture is uncommon.

  • B. Sideroblastic anaemia — Correct. Classically produces a dimorphic blood film.

  • C. Beta thalassaemia — Typically shows a uniform microcytic hypochromic picture with target cells.

  • D. Iron deficiency anaemia — Produces a uniform microcytic hypochromic blood picture unless after treatment.

High-yield Recall

Blood Film Finding Common Association
Dimorphic blood picture Sideroblastic anaemia
Microcytic hypochromic cells Iron deficiency anaemia, thalassaemia
Macro-ovalocytes Megaloblastic anaemia
Target cells Thalassaemia, liver disease
Spherocytes Hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

Exam pearl: The classical association of a dimorphic blood picture in examinations is sideroblastic anaemia.

Medicine-09.question: ২৪) LMWHs preferentially augment antithrombin activity against factor
Medicine-09.exp:
Low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWHs) (e.g., enoxaparin, dalteparin) bind to antithrombin (AT III) and preferentially inhibit Factor Xa. Due to their shorter polysaccharide chain, they have much less activity against thrombin (Factor IIa) than unfractionated heparin.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Factor Xa — Correct. LMWH predominantly enhances antithrombin-mediated inhibition of Factor Xa.

  • B. Factor X — Inactive precursor; LMWH inhibits the activated form (Xa).

  • C. Factor Va — Not the primary target of LMWH.

  • D. Factor IXa — Antithrombin can inhibit IXa, but LMWH has its principal effect on Factor Xa.

High-yield Recall

Drug Main Target
LMWH Factor Xa > Factor IIa (thrombin)
Unfractionated heparin Factor Xa = Factor IIa
Fondaparinux Selective Factor Xa inhibitor
Direct thrombin inhibitors (e.g., dabigatran) Factor IIa

Exam pearl:

  • LMWH → Anti-Xa predominates (anti-Xa : anti-IIa ≈ 2–4 : 1).

  • Unfractionated heparin inhibits both Factor Xa and thrombin (Factor IIa) equally.
